item.title: JavaScript Function Named Parameters Simulation Techniques
item.description:
“JavaScript Function Named Parameters Simulation Techniques”

How can developers effectively manage functions with numerous parameters in JavaScript, especially when seeking the clarity of named arguments found in other languages, while maintaining code readability and good IDE integration? Traditional JavaScript relies heavily on positional arguments, which can lead to confusion when functions have many inputs. Several techniques exist to mimic named parameters, utilizing modern syntax, object manipulation, or even legacy parsing.

item.title: Python Positional-Only Parameters Explained: The Role of the Forward Slash (/)
item.description:
“Python Positional-Only Parameters Explained: The Role of the Forward Slash (/)”

The appearance of a forward slash (/) within a function’s argument list explicitly marks all preceding parameters as positional-only. This means these arguments can only be supplied based on their position during a function call and cannot be passed using their parameter names as keyword arguments.

The Mechanics of Positional-Only Enforcement

This feature became a formal part of the Python language specification starting with Python 3.8, rooted in PEP 570 – Python Positional-Only Parameters. Prior to this, the syntax was reserved for potential future inclusion, as outlined in PEP 457.

item.title: R Language Ellipsis (...) Usage: list() vs substitute() Differences
item.description:
“R Language Ellipsis (…) Usage: list() vs substitute() Differences”

When creating flexible functions in R, the ellipsis operator (...) allows a function to accept a variable number of arguments. However, how these arguments are captured—whether evaluated or unevaluated—is critical for the function’s behavior. Two primary methods emerge for extracting these arguments: the straightforward list(...) and the more intricate as.list(substitute(list(...)))[-1L]. This detailed breakdown examines the mechanics and practical implications of each approach.

item.title: Solved: How to Master Python Function Arguments with `*args` and `**kwargs`
item.description:
“Solved: How to Master Python Function Arguments with *args and **kwargs”

Defining Functions with Variable Positional Arguments (*args)

The *args syntax captures an arbitrary number of positional arguments passed to a function. These arguments are then accessible within the function body as a tuple. This is particularly useful when the exact count of positional inputs might vary.

Consider a function designed to display multiple values:

def print_all_items(*args_collection):
    """Prints each item provided as a positional argument."""
    for item_data in args_collection:
        print(item_data)

print_all_items(101)
